title: Opening and resting the Granth
hook: the Granth is opened at dawn and put to rest at night

segments.voice: Yesterday, in the gurdwara: no idols, no seat higher than the Granth, heads covered for all. Your line was no one above the word. Where did you choose the floor? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-seven.

Before the sangat arrives, a small group crosses the hall. One person walks in the middle with something wrapped in cloth, held up with great care. Another walks beside, waving a whisk over it. A third waits at the raised seat, smoothing the cloths. For Sikhs, what is being carried is the Guru, and so a strange, tender set of questions follows. Where does the Guru spend the night? Who wakes the Guru up? Yesterday we saw the raised seat at the front of the hall. Today we watch what happens on it at the two edges of the day.
screen: `CARRIED ACROSS THE HALL.` → `FOR SIKHS, THE GRANTH IS THE GURU.` → `THE TWO EDGES OF THE DAY.`

segments.voice: The morning word is prakash. In Punjabi it means light, or appearing. In the gurdwara it names the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib for the day. In the early morning the Granth is brought to its raised seat, carried with care, in larger gurdwaras on someone's head. An Ardas is said. The cloths are drawn back. The Granth is opened, and a passage is read from it, a custom we'll come to soon. For Sikhs, from then on, the Guru is present in the hall. In paraphrase, the code says the Granth should be opened in the gurdwara each day, and not kept closed without good reason. The evening word is sukhasan, a seat of ease, of rest. After the night prayers, the Granth is closed, wrapped in its cloths, called rumalas, and carried to a place of rest, in some gurdwaras its own room. The hall goes quiet. In the morning it all begins again. Look at the shape of that. It's the shape of a day lived by a person. Woken gently. Present and attended through the hours. Then laid down to rest with care at night. Some Sikh families who keep a Granth at home in its own room do the same, morning and night. It's easy to treat a ritual like this as fuss. But the care is the teaching. How you open a thing and how you put it down tell you what it is to you. A Sikh doesn't drop the Guru on a table at dawn and leave it open, unattended, until it's forgotten. The word is opened in light, and rested in ease. Open and rest.
screen: `PRAKASH: LIGHT, APPEARING.` · `OPENED AT DAWN WITH AN ARDAS.` · `SUKHASAN: A SEAT OF REST.` · `THE CARE IS THE TEACHING.` · then, large: `OPEN AND REST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open and close your day gently. Settle, and breathe. Think about how this morning began. Was it opened, or did it just crash in? Then think ahead to tonight. How will you lay it down? Choose one small act for each edge. A slow breath before you reach for anything in the morning. A light turned off on purpose at night, with the day set down. If you pray, you can let the first and last words of the day be the Guru's. Rest with that until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Prakash. Light, appearing: the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib for the day. Its evening partner is sukhasan, the seat of rest. Today's word.
Your line: open and rest. Tonight, put one thing down with care, a book, a tool, a phone, the day itself, the way you'd want to be put to rest. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: In gurdwaras the Guru Granth Sahib is opened in the morning with Ardas (prakash) and, after the night prayers, closed, wrapped in rumalas and taken to rest (sukhasan); some families with a Granth at home do the same.

original.note: Punjabi: light, appearing; the Granth opened and present for the day.

trapdoor: what you thought: prakash is just opening a big book.
what it means: the morning opening of the Guru Granth Sahib with Ardas; at night it is closed and rested in sukhasan.
what a scholar hears: light and a seat of ease: the Granth is handled as the living Guru, woken and rested, never just shelved.

notes: The code is paraphrased as saying the Granth should be opened in the gurdwara daily and not kept closed without good reason; please confirm.
Prakash glossed as 'light, appearing' and sukhasan as 'a seat of ease, of rest': word meanings, not etymologies; please confirm.

The description of the ceremony (carried, in larger gurdwaras on the head; Ardas; cloths drawn back; a passage read; closed after the night prayers, wrapped in rumalas, taken to a resting place, in some gurdwaras its own room) is a general description of practice; please confirm.
'Some Sikh families who keep a Granth at home in its own room do the same': please confirm.
